title: Distributed Phase Tags: A Locality-Preserving Realification Compiler for Misty-State Quantum Programs
abstract: Complex amplitudes can be simulated over real Hilbert spaces by adjoining a two-dimensional real/imaginary degree of freedom. In a multipartite program, however, one globally shared phase tag is not a locality-preserving program transformation: every party would have to act on the same auxiliary system. We recast the distributed real simulation of multipartite quantum mechanics as a syntax-directed compiler into a real misty-state intermediate language. For $n$ parties we give explicit phase-reference codewords $|0\rangle_{P_n}$ and $|1\rangle_{P_n}$ on $n$ local tags and prove that the same real operator $J=XZ$ on any single tag realizes the logical action of multiplication by $i$. If a complex party-local gate is $A=A_R+iA_I$, its real translation is \[   \widehat A_j=A_R\otimes I+A_I\otimes J_j, \] which acts only on party $j$'s data and local phase tag. We prove an intertwining theorem for arbitrary finite party-local pure-state circuits, exact preservation of computational-basis measurement probabilities, preservation of the run-time interaction graph, and one-rebit-per-party overhead. For the canonical three-party GHZ program, the translation lies entirely inside the ordinary black-and-white misty gate fragment: controlled-$J$ replaces the complex phase operation, while the invariant $J_jJ_k|0\rangle_P=-|0\rangle_P$ transfers the required branch sign. This yields a short correctness proof for all four promised GHZ inputs and explains the earlier 64-path cancellation calculation at a single logical phase-code boundary. We distinguish this program realification problem from the weaker task of finding any real strategy with the same correlations, and state precisely which parts are known real-Hilbert-space simulation and which parts belong to the misty-language compilation layer developed here.
summary: This paper presents a compiler that translates complex quantum circuits into an equivalent, locality-preserving computation using only real-valued operations within a 'misty-state' framework. By encoding the imaginary component using local phase tags, it successfully simulates complex quantum gates while guaranteeing the preservation of measurement probabilities and the interaction structure. This provides a powerful theoretical tool for realizing complex quantum algorithms on hardware restricted to real Hamiltonians.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of simulating complex quantum computations, which naturally involve complex amplitudes, using only real-valued operations while preserving locality in a multipartite setting.
main_result: It develops a locality-preserving compiler that translates complex quantum circuits into a real 'misty-state' intermediate language, proving that the resulting real circuit maintains the original computational-basis measurement probabilities.
method: The core method involves recasting the simulation into a syntax-directed compiler that encodes the complex structure using local, auxiliary phase tags (rebits) for each party.
model_or_system: The model is multipartite quantum computation. The simulation is achieved by adjoining a two-dimensional real/imaginary degree of freedom to the Hilbert space, leading to the 'misty-state' formalism.
key_observables: Computational-basis measurement probabilities, the run-time interaction graph, and the overhead (proven to be one rebit per party).
important_parameters: The number of parties ($n$), the local phase-reference codewords ($|0angle_{Pn}, |1angle_{Pn}$), and the structure of the complex gate $A = A_R + iA_I$.
main_assumptions: The proof is restricted to finite party-local pure-state circuits followed by computational-basis measurements; extensions to mixed states or general measurements require different semantics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the compiler architecture, showing how nonlocal phase codes are prepared locally, and demonstrate the logical structure of the GHZ state translation using local $J$ operators.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, defines the realification map and the compiler rules (e.g., $A_j 	o A_R \otimes I + A_I \otimes J_j$), proves the intertwining theorem for general circuits, and applies the framework to the canonical three-party GHZ program.
why_interesting: For theorists working on open quantum systems or quantum computation, this work provides a rigorous, resource-aware method for simulating complex quantum dynamics using only real physical resources, which is crucial for physical implementations.
